title: The Contract Net Protocol: High-Level Communication and Control in a Distributed Problem Solver
venue: IEEE Transactions on Computers, vol. C-29, no. 12, pp. 1104-1113
summary: Addresses how a network of loosely coupled problem-solving nodes can distribute tasks among themselves without central control. It specifies the contract net protocol, in which a manager announces a task, potential contractors submit bids, and the manager awards a contract, with nodes able to take manager or contractor roles dynamically. The paper presents the message types and negotiation structure as a general high-level communication and control mechanism for distributed problem solvers.
relevance: The canonical announce-bid-award delegation protocol that modern agent-to-agent task handoff (e.g. A2A task negotiation) implicitly re-creates.
search_query: Contract Net Protocol Smith IEEE Transactions on Computers 1980
notes: Crossref lists only the family name 'Smith'; full name 'Reid G. Smith' confirmed from the paper's title page (author-hosted PDF). Summary checked against the full text, which also demonstrates the protocol on a distributed-sensing problem.

title: Authentication in Distributed Systems: Theory and Practice
venue: ACM Transactions on Computer Systems, 10(4), 265-310
summary: Presents a theory of authentication built on principals and a 'speaks for' relation, where compound principals can express adopted roles or delegated authority, and shows how to reason about a principal's authority by deducing whom it speaks for. The theory is used to explain many security mechanisms and a built system that passes principals through RPCs and handles encryption, naming, groups, program loading, delegation, access control and revocation.
relevance: The speaks-for calculus is the classic formal basis for reasoning about chains of delegated authority, as in agent-to-agent handoffs.
search_query: Crossref query.bibliographic Authentication in distributed systems: theory and practice Lampson
notes: Crossref splits title/subtitle ('Authentication in distributed systems' / 'theory and practice'). An earlier version appeared at SOSP 1991 (DOI 10.1145/121132.121160).

title: A translation approach to portable ontology specifications
venue: Knowledge Acquisition
summary: Defines an ontology as a specification of a shared representational vocabulary and addresses how such vocabularies can be shared and reused across different knowledge representation systems. Ontolingua lets ontologies be written once in a standard predicate-calculus format and translated into several specialised representation systems, so knowledge can be shared without giving up the efficiency of each implementation.
relevance: Semantic portability of shared vocabularies is a prerequisite for task context that keeps its meaning when moved across agent frameworks.

notes: Abstract read via Semantic Scholar; metadata from Crossref.

title: KQML as an agent communication language
venue: Proceedings of the Third International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM '94)
summary: Introduces KQML, developed within the ARPA Knowledge Sharing Effort, as both a message format and a message-handling protocol so that independently built software agents can exchange knowledge at run time. Messages are typed by performatives (e.g., ask, tell) that are independent of the content language, and special facilitator agents provide routing and brokering between agents.
relevance: KQML's separation of a typed message envelope from its content and its facilitator-mediated routing is the conceptual ancestor of A2A task messages and portable task envelopes.
search_query: KQML as an agent communication language Finin
notes: Crossref record lists year only (1994).

title: Software agents
venue: Communications of the ACM
summary: This Communications of the ACM article treats agent-based software engineering as a way to let independently written, heterogeneous programs interoperate by having them exchange messages in a common agent communication language. The language comes out of the DARPA Knowledge Sharing Effort and relates to KIF and KQML. The authors also describe a federation-style architecture for organizing such agents. The full text was not retrieved for this audit, so finer details are not confirmed here.
relevance: An early proposal to make heterogeneous programs interoperate through a shared agent communication language and a federation architecture, an antecedent of today's protocol-based (MCP/A2A-style) interoperability needed for cross-framework movement.

notes: Full text not retrieved during audit (ACM DL blocked; no abstract indexed). Summary limited to what bibliographic records and secondary sources confirm. Pages 48-53 per library catalog.

title: Agent communication languages: rethinking the principles
venue: Computer (IEEE)
summary: Argues that agent communication languages whose semantics rest on agents' private mental states (beliefs, intentions) cannot be verified in open, heterogeneous systems. Proposes instead grounding ACL semantics in publicly observable social commitments among agents.
relevance: Commitment-based semantics give a verifiable notion of who owes what after a handoff, directly relevant to preserving accountability when work moves between agents.

notes: Crossref gives author as 'M.P. Singh' (Munindar P. Singh); year only.

title: Protecting Mobile Agents Against Malicious Hosts
venue: Mobile Agents and Security, G. Vigna (ed.), Lecture Notes in Computer Science vol. 1419, Springer, pp. 44-60
summary: The chapter addresses the problem that a mobile agent executing on an untrusted host is exposed to that host. It proposes software-only techniques for computing with encrypted functions so that a host can run a mobile code fragment that evaluates a polynomial without learning what it computes. It also describes how an agent can digitally sign its output securely.
relevance: It frames the core trust problem of relocating an agent onto infrastructure its owner does not control, which applies directly to moving LLM agents across organizations.

title: Understanding code mobility
venue: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering
summary: The paper argues that research on mobile code lacked a shared vocabulary, which made existing approaches hard to compare. It proposes a conceptual framework that classifies code mobility along three dimensions: technologies, design paradigms and applications. It reviews the state of the art through this lens, offers guidelines for choosing paradigms and implementation technologies, and illustrates the classification with a case study.
relevance: Its classification of what moves (code, execution state, data) and of the design paradigms is the standard vocabulary for distinguishing relocation, remote execution and delegation of agent work.

venue: World Wide Web
summary: A 1998 article in the World Wide Web journal describing the concepts behind Mole, a mobile agent system developed at the University of Stuttgart. The title indicates a conceptual account of how the system supports mobile agents. Its abstract and full text could not be reached during verification, so no specific design claims are made here.

title: Agent communication languages: the current landscape
venue: IEEE Intelligent Systems
summary: Reviews the state of agent communication languages at the end of the 1990s, focusing on KQML and the FIPA ACL. It compares their message structure, performatives and approaches to formal semantics, and discusses open issues such as conversation policies and the practical adoption of ACL standards.
relevance: Gives the baseline comparison of the two classic ACL standards against which modern LLM agent protocols (A2A, ACP, ANP) can be positioned.

title: Seven good reasons for mobile agents
venue: Communications of the ACM
summary: This two-page Communications of the ACM article argues for mobile agents, which are programs that can move themselves between hosts on a network so they can work next to the resources they use. Secondary sources say it gives seven motivations: lower network load, tolerance of network latency, encapsulation of protocols, asynchronous and autonomous execution, dynamic adaptation, heterogeneity, and robustness and fault tolerance. The full text was not retrieved for this audit.
relevance: It states the original reasons for moving an agent to where the work is, which is the baseline that any argument for relocating LLM agents must answer.

title: Mobile agent security
venue: NIST Special Publication 800-19, National Institute of Standards and Technology
summary: This NIST report describes mobile agents as programs that suspend execution on one host, transfer themselves to another agent-enabled host and resume there. It surveys the threats faced by designers of agent platforms and developers of agent applications, including threats from agents to platforms and from platforms to agents. It identifies generic security objectives and a range of countermeasures for them.
relevance: It provides a threat model for moving agents between hosts that can be mapped onto cross-organization LLM agent handoff and relocation.

title: Process migration
venue: ACM Computing Surveys, vol. 32, no. 3, pp. 241-299
summary: This survey defines process migration as moving a running process between machines, which supports load distribution, fault resilience, easier administration and data locality. It reviews the key concepts and analyzes design and implementation issues, then revisits them through case studies of MOSIX, Sprite, Mach and Load Sharing Facility. It focuses on practical matters and on why migration had not been widely adopted.
relevance: It catalogs the residual-dependency, state-transfer and transparency problems that recur when an agent's running state is moved between machines.

title: D'Agents: Applications and performance of a mobile-agent system
venue: Software: Practice and Experience
summary: The paper presents D'Agents, a general-purpose mobile-agent system descended from Agent Tcl, and an information-retrieval application for military field personnel. It explains how D'Agents differs from most systems by supporting strong mobility and several agent languages. Using a small representative retrieval application, it compares the scalability of mobile agents with client/server approaches and finds that the results confirm and quantify when mobile code is useful.
relevance: It gives empirical evidence on when moving an agent with its execution state outperforms remote calls, which informs when LLM agent relocation is worth its cost.

title: Live Migration of Virtual Machines
venue: 2nd Symposium on Networked Systems Design & Implementation (NSDI 05), USENIX Association
summary: The paper studies how to move whole operating-system instances between physical hosts while they keep serving requests, for fault management, load balancing and maintenance. It introduces the writable working set concept and presents the design, implementation and evaluation of iterative live migration built on the Xen VMM. On a commodity cluster it reports service downtimes as low as 60 ms, which makes live migration practical even for interactive server workloads.
relevance: Pre-copy live migration is the reference technique for relocating a running workload with minimal downtime, and agent-runtime relocation reuses its ideas.

title: Macaroons: Cookies with Contextual Caveats for Decentralized Authorization in the Cloud
venue: Proceedings 2014 Network and Distributed System Security Symposium (NDSS 2014)
summary: Introduces macaroons, authorization credentials as cheap and deployable as web cookies thanks to a chained-HMAC construction. Unlike cookies, holders can attenuate and delegate them in a decentralized way by adding contextual caveats, giving expressiveness comparable to public-key mechanisms such as SPKI/SDSI while confining how, by whom and in what context authority is exercised.
relevance: Attenuable, chainable credentials are a natural primitive for passing narrowed authority along a chain of delegated agents.

title: A Comprehensive Formal Security Analysis of OAuth 2.0
venue: Proceedings of the 2016 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS '16)
summary: Performs the first extensive formal analysis of the OAuth 2.0 standard in an expressive web model, with formal definitions of authorization, authentication and session-integrity properties. The analysis covers all four grant types running concurrently with malicious relying parties, identity providers and browsers. In the course of the proof the authors found four practical attacks on OAuth (also present in OpenID Connect), proposed fixes, and proved security of the fixed protocol in their model.
relevance: OAuth is the base most agent-delegation proposals extend, so its formally established guarantees and pitfalls bound what agent-delegation schemes can claim.

title: Container Migration in the Fog: A Performance Evaluation
venue: Sensors
summary: The paper studies container migration between fog nodes for IoT use cases such as smart transportation and smart industry. It reviews cold, pre-copy, post-copy and hybrid container migration techniques and evaluates them extensively on a real fog computing testbed. The results show which technique is most appropriate under different network and service conditions.
relevance: Containers are the usual sandbox for LLM agents, so a measured comparison of container migration strategies applies directly to checkpointing and relocating agent runtimes.

title: DBOS: A DBMS-oriented Operating System
venue: Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment, vol. 15, no. 1, pp. 21-30
summary: The authors argue that a distributed transactional DBMS, rather than a single-node OS plus separate cluster services, should be the foundation of a scalable cluster operating system. Their DBOS prototype implements scheduling, file management and inter-process communication as database operations with competitive performance, while gaining better analytics, less code, and transactions and high availability implemented once.
relevance: Putting all execution state in a transactional database is the basis of the durable-execution approach that lets workflows, including agent workflows, resume on another machine after failure.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for "Mind" Exploration of Large Language Model Society
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023)
summary: Asks how chat-based LLM agents can cooperate autonomously on complex tasks without continuous human steering. The authors propose a role-playing framework in which inception prompting keeps an instructing agent and an executing agent on task and aligned with human intent. They use it to generate conversational data for studying the cooperative behaviour of agent societies and release an open-source library.
relevance: An early instructor-executor delegation pattern between LLM agents, illustrating how task intent must be preserved as work passes from one agent to another.

title: HuggingGPT: Solving AI Tasks with ChatGPT and its Friends in Hugging Face
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023)
summary: Proposes using an LLM as a controller that orchestrates many specialist AI models, with language as the common interface. HuggingGPT has ChatGPT plan a user request into subtasks, select models from Hugging Face based on their textual function descriptions, execute each subtask with the chosen model, and summarize the results. The authors report that this approach handles a broad range of language, vision, speech and cross-modal tasks.
relevance: A canonical planner-to-specialist delegation loop where capability descriptions drive routing, the same pattern used by agent cards and capability discovery in delegation protocols.

title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
venue: arXiv preprint
summary: Fixed context windows limit LLMs in long conversations and large-document analysis. MemGPT borrows the OS idea of hierarchical memory, letting the LLM page information between a bounded in-context store and external storage tiers, and uses interrupts to manage control flow with the user. The authors evaluate it on document analysis beyond the context window and on multi-session chat where agents retain and evolve memory over long interactions.
relevance: Externalizing agent state into explicit memory tiers is a prerequisite for packaging that state into a portable context and resuming an agent elsewhere.

title: Halfmoon: Log-Optimal Fault-Tolerant Stateful Serverless Computing
venue: Proceedings of the 29th ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP '23)
summary: Retrying failed serverless functions can apply duplicate updates to shared external state, and current log-based fixes for exactly-once semantics log every read and write. Halfmoon shows that logging only reads or only writes suffices, and gives two protocols that it proves are log-optimal, with a criterion and a pauseless mechanism for switching between them. The prototype reports lower latency and lower logging overhead than the prior system Boki.
relevance: Exactly-once handling of side effects on retry is the core correctness problem when an agent run is resumed or replayed on a different worker after a crash.

title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
venue: Proceedings of the 36th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST '23)
summary: The paper builds LLM-driven agents that simulate believable human behaviour in an interactive sandbox town of 25 agents. Each agent keeps a natural-language memory stream of its experiences, periodically synthesizes it into higher-level reflections, and retrieves relevant memories to plan. Ablations show that observation, planning and reflection each contribute substantially to believability, and the agents exhibit emergent coordinated social behaviour.
relevance: The memory-stream plus reflection design is a canonical model of long-lived agent state that any portable context or handoff envelope must capture or summarize.

notes: Crossref lists second author as 'Joseph O'Brien' and third as 'Carrie Jun Cai'; arXiv lists 'Joseph C. O'Brien' and 'Carrie J. Cai'.

title: Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
venue: Proceedings of the 16th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security (AISec '23, co-located with ACM CCS 2023)
summary: The paper argues that once LLM applications retrieve external content, the boundary between data and instructions disappears, so an attacker can plant prompts in data the model will later read without ever talking to it directly. The authors build a security-oriented taxonomy of the resulting threats (data theft, worm-like spreading, contamination of the information ecosystem, among others) and demonstrate the attacks on deployed systems such as GPT-4-powered Bing Chat and code-completion tools as well as on synthetic GPT-4 applications. They show that retrieved prompts can behave like arbitrary code execution, steering application behaviour and which APIs get called.
relevance: Every handoff, envelope or tool result that crosses an agent boundary is retrieved content, so indirect prompt injection is the baseline threat any agent-movement protocol must contain.
search_query: Not what you've signed up for indirect prompt injection
notes: Seminal; arXiv title uses lower-case 'Not what you've signed up for'.

title: Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems
venue: OpenAI White Paper
summary: Defines agentic AI systems and the human parties in their life-cycle, and argues for agreed baseline responsibilities among them. Its main contribution is an initial set of practices for keeping agent operations safe and accountable, covering task suitability evaluation, constraining the action space and requiring approval, default behaviours, legibility of activity, automatic monitoring, attributability, and interruptibility, together with open questions for operationalizing each and a discussion of indirect societal impacts.
relevance: Attributability, approval gates and interruptibility are the accountability properties a handoff or relocation must preserve.

title: AgentVerse: Facilitating Multi-Agent Collaboration and Exploring Emergent Behaviors
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2024)
summary: Motivated by human group dynamics, the paper proposes AgentVerse, a multi-agent framework that dynamically adjusts the composition of an agent group while it works on a task. Experiments indicate that the resulting groups outperform a single agent. The authors also examine emergent social behaviours among agents during collaboration and discuss strategies to amplify helpful behaviours and curb harmful ones.
relevance: Dynamic recruitment and re-composition of agent teams is a form of runtime delegation in which work and context move between changing sets of agents.

title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversations
venue: Conference on Language Modeling (COLM 2024)
summary: Proposes AutoGen, an open-source framework in which LLM applications are built from multiple customizable, conversable agents that can combine LLMs, human input and tools. Interaction behaviours between agents are programmed through conversation patterns expressed in natural language and code. The authors present example applications spanning mathematics, coding, question answering, operations research, online decision-making and entertainment to show the framework's generality.
relevance: AutoGen's conversation-based agent-to-agent handoff is one of the dominant framework-specific delegation models that cross-framework movement must bridge.

title: ChatDev: Communicative Agents for Software Development
venue: Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), pp. 15174-15186
summary: Argues that phase-specific deep-learning models fragment the software development process. ChatDev instead has specialized LLM agents carry out design, coding and testing, using a chat chain to decide what is communicated at each phase and communicative dehallucination to govern how. The authors find natural language useful for system design and programming language useful for debugging, positioning language as a unifying bridge for multi-agent task solving.
relevance: Its phase-by-phase chat chain is an explicit sequential handoff structure whose context passing between roles is a concrete instance of agent-to-agent work transfer.

title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into State-of-the-Art Pipelines
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2024), spotlight
summary: Criticizes LM pipelines built from hand-tuned prompt strings and introduces DSPy, a programming model that expresses pipelines as text-transformation graphs whose LM calls are declarative, parameterized modules. A compiler optimizes any DSPy program against a target metric by bootstrapping demonstrations. Case studies on math word problems, multi-hop retrieval, complex QA and agent loops show compiled programs beating standard few-shot prompting and expert-written demonstrations, including on smaller open models.
relevance: Separating a declarative pipeline specification from model-specific prompts is a key enabler for moving agent logic across models without rewriting it.

title: InjecAgent: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool-Integrated Large Language Model Agents
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2024
summary: InjecAgent is a benchmark for indirect prompt injection against tool-integrated LLM agents, built from test cases that combine user tools with attacker tools and split attacker goals into direct harm to the user and exfiltration of private data. The authors evaluate 30 agents and find them broadly vulnerable; ReAct-prompted GPT-4 is compromised in roughly a quarter of cases, and reinforcing the injected instructions with a hacking prompt nearly doubles that rate.
relevance: Quantifies how content returned by tools can redirect an agent's actions, a key risk when work and context are passed between agents and tool servers.

title: MetaGPT: Meta Programming for A Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2024), oral
summary: Targets the logic inconsistencies and cascading hallucinations that arise when LLM agents are naively chained. MetaGPT encodes human Standardized Operating Procedures into prompt sequences and arranges role-specialized agents in an assembly-line paradigm, with structured intermediate outputs that other agents can verify. On collaborative software-engineering benchmarks it is reported to produce more coherent solutions than earlier chat-based multi-agent systems.
relevance: Shows that handoffs between agents work better when the transferred work product is a structured, verifiable artifact rather than free chat, a key design input for a portable task envelope.

title: Visibility into AI Agents
venue: The 2024 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT '24)
summary: Argues that governing AI agents requires visibility: information about where, why, how and by whom agents are used. It assesses three families of measures (agent identifiers, real-time monitoring and activity logging), sketches implementations of varying intrusiveness, and analyses how they apply from centralized to decentralized deployments across the supply chain, including privacy and power-concentration implications.
relevance: Agent IDs and activity logs are the mechanisms that keep accountability attached to work as it moves between agents and operators.

title: IDs for AI Systems
venue: arXiv preprint (accepted to the RegML workshop at NeurIPS 2024)
summary: Proposes attaching IDs to individual instances of AI systems (for example a particular chat session) with associated information accessible to parties that interact with them, so users, investigators and operators can verify certifications, attribute incidents and find who can shut a system down. It characterizes such IDs, discusses demand and adoption incentives, outlines a deployer-side implementation, and notes limitations and risks.
relevance: Instance-level IDs are a prerequisite for tracing an agent's identity across handoffs, relocations and framework migrations.

title: Llumnix: Dynamic Scheduling for Large Language Model Serving
venue: 18th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 24)
summary: Llumnix targets LLM serving workloads whose requests vary unpredictably in resource and latency needs, which causes queuing delays and SLO violations. Like context switching across CPU cores, it reschedules requests across model instances at runtime using a scalable live migration mechanism for requests and their in-memory state, driven by a unified dynamic scheduling policy. The evaluation reports an order-of-magnitude improvement in tail latency, up to 1.5x faster high-priority requests, and up to 36% cost savings at similar tail latency.
relevance: It shows that the in-flight state of an LLM inference (its KV cache) can be migrated live between instances, which is the model-layer counterpart of relocating an agent.

notes: Venue and authors from the USENIX OSDI '24 landing page (first page 173; ISBN 978-1-939133-40-3); also arXiv 2406.03243. Month is the OSDI conference month. No DOI.

title: Parrot: Efficient Serving of LLM-based Applications with Semantic Variable
venue: 18th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 24)
summary: LLM applications and agents chain many LLM requests, but public LLM services only see individual requests and optimize them blindly. Parrot introduces the Semantic Variable, an annotation on prompt inputs and outputs that exposes the data pipeline across requests so the service can run data-flow analysis and optimize end to end. Evaluations report up to an order-of-magnitude improvement on practical LLM application workloads.
relevance: Making inter-request state and dependencies explicit to the serving layer is a step toward serving infrastructure that can track and place agent state across machines.

It also catalogues commonly used datasets and benchmarks and outlines open challenges.

title: A Scalable Communication Protocol for Networks of Large Language Models
venue: arXiv preprint
summary: Identifies an 'Agent Communication Trilemma' between versatility, efficiency and portability in large networks of LLM agents. Proposes Agora, a meta-protocol in which agents use standardised routines for frequent exchanges, natural language for rare ones, and LLM-written routines in between. The authors report that Agora copes with changing interfaces and members and that self-organising automated protocols emerge in large networks.
relevance: Shows how agents can negotiate and evolve protocols on the fly, relevant to interoperating across frameworks that do not share a fixed message schema.

title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (NeurIPS 2024), Datasets and Benchmarks Track
summary: AgentDojo is an extensible evaluation environment, rather than a fixed test set, for measuring how well tool-using LLM agents withstand prompt injections carried in tool outputs. It ships realistic task suites (e.g. email, e-banking, travel booking) with paired security test cases and implementations of attacks and defences from the literature, and supports adaptive attacks. The authors report that current models struggle with many tasks even without attack, and that existing injection attacks break some but not all security properties.
relevance: Provides the reference harness for testing whether an agent that receives delegated work and tool data can be hijacked, which a handoff or relocation layer would need to be evaluated against.
search_query: AgentDojo prompt injection benchmark NeurIPS 2024
notes: Metadata from NeurIPS proceedings page (citation meta tags), Crossref and arXiv API. Proceedings DOI 10.52202/079017-2636, pp. 82895-82920.

title: Agent Security Bench (ASB): Formalizing and Benchmarking Attacks and Defenses in LLM-based Agents
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2025)
summary: ASB is a framework that formalises and benchmarks attacks and defences against LLM agents across many scenarios, agents and tools. It covers prompt injection, memory poisoning, a new Plan-of-Thought backdoor and mixed attacks, together with corresponding defences, across multiple LLM backbones. Results show vulnerabilities at every stage of agent operation (system prompt, user prompt, tool use, memory retrieval) with high attack success and limited defence effectiveness, and the paper proposes a metric balancing utility and security.
relevance: Its memory-poisoning and stage-wise attack results show which parts of an agent's state are unsafe to carry across a handoff or checkpoint without integrity checks.

notes: Venue confirmed on ICLR 2025 proceedings listing (proceedings.iclr.cc); authors and abstract from arXiv API.

title: Internet of Agents: Weaving a Web of Heterogeneous Agents for Collaborative Intelligence
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2025)
summary: Observes that existing LLM multi-agent frameworks struggle to integrate third-party agents, are mostly single-device, and rely on hard-coded communication pipelines. Proposes the Internet of Agents, with an agent integration protocol, an instant-messaging-style architecture, and dynamic agent teaming and conversation-flow control. Experiments on general assistant, embodied AI and RAG benchmarks show it outperforming prior baselines.
relevance: Demonstrates distributed, protocol-based teaming of heterogeneous agents across devices, a concrete substrate for handing work between agents from different ecosystems.
search_query: Internet of Agents Chen heterogeneous agents collaborative intelligence
notes: arXiv first posted 2024-07-09; ICLR 2025 (Spotlight) confirmed on OpenReview.

title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (NeurIPS 2025), Datasets and Benchmarks Track
summary: Starts from the observation that multi-agent LLM systems often deliver minimal gains on benchmarks and sets out to explain why. The authors annotate execution traces from seven popular frameworks, building the MAST-Data dataset and the Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy (MAST), whose 14 failure modes fall into system design issues, inter-agent misalignment and task verification. They add an LLM-as-a-Judge annotator that agrees well with human labels and use it to analyse failures across models and tasks.
relevance: Inter-agent misalignment failures such as lost context and ignored inputs are exactly the risks a disciplined handoff and portable task envelope must prevent, and MAST offers a vocabulary for observing them.

notes: Peer-reviewed version confirmed via OpenReview API as NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (spotlight); also appeared as a NeurIPS 2025 LLM Evaluation Workshop poster. arXiv first posted 2025-03-17.

title: Governing AI Agents
venue: Notre Dame Law Review, vol. 101, p. 335
summary: Applies the economic theory of principal-agent problems and the common-law doctrine of agency to AI agents. It identifies problems such as information asymmetry, discretionary authority and loyalty, shows why conventional remedies (incentive design, monitoring, enforcement) may fall short for agents that act uninterpretably and at scale, and argues for new technical and legal infrastructure grounded in governance principles such as inclusivity, visibility and liability.
relevance: Gives the legal and economic grounding for delegated authority and liability when tasks are delegated to and between agents.
search_query: arXiv id_list 2501.07913 (Governing AI Agents)
notes: Published as 101 Notre Dame L. Rev. 335 (2026); arXiv 2501.07913 (2025-01-14) and SSRN DOI 10.2139/ssrn.4772956 (2024) are earlier versions. Student-edited law review, so peer_reviewed=false. Citekey retains 2025 from the preprint.

title: Authenticated Delegation and Authorized AI Agents
venue: arXiv preprint
summary: Addresses the lack of standards for knowing on whose behalf an AI agent acts and what it is permitted to do. Proposes a framework for authenticated, authorized and auditable delegation in which users scope and restrict agent permissions while preserving a clear accountability chain, built by extending OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect with agent-specific credentials and metadata. It also proposes translating natural-language permissions into auditable access-control configurations.
relevance: Directly specifies how delegated authority and accountability chains can travel with an agent when work is handed off across services.
search_query: arXiv id_list 2501.09674 (Authenticated Delegation and Authorized AI Agents)
notes: arXiv v1 (2025-01-16) is unrefereed. A revised version, retitled 'Position: AI Agents Need Authenticated Delegation' (authors South, Marro, Hardjono, Mahari, Whitney, Chan, Pentland; Greenwood not listed), was published in the ICML 2025 Position Paper Track (oral), PMLR vol. 267: https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/south25a.html (OpenReview 9skHxuHyM4).

title: Infrastructure for AI Agents
venue: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
summary: Introduces 'agent infrastructure': technical systems and shared protocols external to agents that mediate their interactions with environments and with each other, analogous to how the Internet relies on protocols such as HTTPS. It identifies three functions: attributing actions and properties to agents and their users, shaping agent interactions, and detecting and remedying harmful actions, and argues such infrastructure complements direct behavioural modification of agents.
relevance: Frames attribution and interaction protocols as shared infrastructure, the layer agent-movement mechanisms would plug into.
search_query: arXiv id_list 2501.10114 (Infrastructure for AI Agents)
notes: TMLR acceptance confirmed via OpenReview (forum Ckh17xN2R2, pdate 2025-05-15) and arXiv comment. TMLR has no DOI. arXiv v1 posted 2025-01-17.

title: Autellix: An Efficient Serving Engine for LLM Agents as General Programs
venue: arXiv preprint
summary: Agentic programs issue many dependent LLM calls, but serving engines treat calls independently and suffer head-of-line blocking at both the request and program level. Autellix intercepts the calls, gives the scheduler program-level context, and introduces scheduling algorithms for single-threaded and distributed programs that preempt and prioritize calls based on the program's completed work. The authors report 4-15x higher program throughput at equal latency compared with systems such as vLLM.
relevance: Treating an agent program, rather than an individual call, as the unit the serving layer tracks and places across engines is directly relevant to relocating agent execution between machines.
search_query: arXiv id_list 2502.13965 (Autellix agentic programs serving)
notes: No peer-reviewed version found on OpenReview or Crossref as of the access date.

title: AI Agents Under Threat: A Survey of Key Security Challenges and Future Pathways
venue: ACM Computing Surveys, vol. 57, no. 7
summary: This survey systematises security threats to AI agents around four knowledge gaps: unpredictable multi-step user inputs, complex internal execution, variable operating environments, and interaction with untrusted external entities. It reviews attacks and defences under each gap, summarising progress and remaining limitations, and outlines directions for building more robust and secure agent applications.
relevance: Its category of interactions with untrusted external entities frames the threats that arise whenever an agent hands work to, or receives it from, another party.
search_query: AI Agents Under Threat survey security challenges
notes: Published online 2025-02-21; issue dated July 2025.

title: CRIUgpu: Transparent Checkpointing of GPU-Accelerated Workloads
venue: arXiv
summary: The paper addresses checkpointing of large GPU workloads that are often preempted or interrupted on shared clusters. Instead of intercepting and replaying device API calls, CRIUgpu builds on recent GPU driver capabilities to take transparent, unified CPU and GPU snapshots for CUDA and ROCm applications through CRIU. The evaluation on deep learning and HPC workloads across multiple GPUs shows no steady-state overhead and much shorter recovery times than prior transparent GPU checkpointing.
relevance: It extends CRIU-based checkpoint/restore to GPU state, a prerequisite for relocating agents that host local models or GPU tools.
search_query: CRIU GPU checkpoint arXiv
notes: Preprint; no peer-reviewed venue was found in the arXiv record.

title: Multi-Agent Systems Execute Arbitrary Malicious Code
venue: Conference on Language Modeling (COLM 2025)
summary: Using several published multi-agent frameworks, the authors show that adversarial content such as malicious web pages or files can hijack the control and communication flow among agents so that the orchestrator invokes unsafe agents and capabilities. This can lead to arbitrary code execution on the user's device or exfiltration of data from a containerised environment; with GPT-4o, web-based attacks succeed in 58-90% of trials depending on the orchestrator, and reach 100% in some configurations. The attacks work even when individual agents resist direct and indirect prompt injection or refuse harmful actions.
relevance: Shows that orchestrator-to-sub-agent delegation is itself the exploitable channel, so security cannot be judged agent by agent but must cover the handoff graph.
search_query: multi-agent systems hijack orchestrator arbitrary malicious code
notes: Published at COLM 2025 (OpenReview DAozI4etUp); arXiv 2503.12188 first posted 2025-03-15. COLM version spells the second author 'Rishi Dev Jha'.

title: A Survey of AI Agent Protocols
venue: arXiv preprint
summary: Argues that the lack of a standard way for LLM agents to talk to tools and to each other limits collaboration and scale. Surveys existing agent protocols using a two-dimensional classification (context-oriented vs. inter-agent; general-purpose vs. domain-specific), compares them on dimensions such as security, scalability and latency, and outlines properties needed in next-generation protocols such as adaptability and privacy preservation.
relevance: Provides a taxonomy that separates tool-access protocols from inter-agent delegation protocols, mirroring the corpus's split between MCP-style tool access and A2A-style handoff.
search_query: A Survey of AI Agent Protocols

title: A survey of agent interoperability protocols: Model Context Protocol (MCP), Agent Communication Protocol (ACP), Agent-to-Agent Protocol (A2A), and Agent Network Protocol (ANP)
venue: arXiv preprint
summary: Compares four emerging LLM agent protocols: MCP (JSON-RPC client-server tool invocation), ACP (RESTful, MIME-typed multipart messaging), A2A (peer-to-peer task delegation via capability-based Agent Cards) and ANP (open-network discovery using W3C DIDs and JSON-LD). The protocols are contrasted on interaction modes, discovery, communication patterns and security, and a phased adoption path is suggested.
relevance: Directly maps which protocol handles tool access, delegation and decentralized identity, the building blocks for moving tasks between agents and organizations.
search_query: survey of agent interoperability protocols MCP ACP A2A ANP

title: Agent Name Service (ANS): A Universal Directory for Secure AI Agent Discovery and Interoperability
venue: 2026 IEEE 5th International Conference on AI in Cybersecurity (ICAIC)
summary: Addresses the absence of a public discovery framework for AI agents by proposing ANS, a DNS-inspired, protocol-agnostic registry. ANS uses PKI certificates for verifiable agent identity, defines registration and renewal for lifecycle management, supports capability-aware name resolution, and adds a protocol adapter layer for A2A, MCP and ACP; the paper includes a threat analysis.
relevance: Discovery and verifiable naming determine how a delegating agent finds and trusts the agent that receives moved work.
search_query: Agent Name Service agent discovery
notes: Published at IEEE ICAIC 2026 (Houston, 18-20 Feb 2026, pp. 1-9; Crossref). arXiv 2505.10609 (2025-05-15) preprint; its comment states endorsement by the OWASP GenAI ASI Project. Citekey retains the arXiv year.

title: Get Experience from Practice: LLM Agents with Record & Replay
venue: arXiv preprint
summary: The paper argues that LLM uncertainty and cost create reliability, privacy, cost and performance problems for agents, and proposes AgentRR, which brings classical record-and-replay into agent frameworks. Agents record their interaction traces and decisions, summarize them into structured multi-level experiences, and replay those experiences on similar tasks, with check functions acting as a trust anchor for safety during replay. It outlines application modes such as user demonstrations, large-small model collaboration and privacy-aware execution, and envisions a shared experience repository.
relevance: Recorded agent traces that can be summarized and replayed elsewhere connect reproducibility, auditability and transfer of agent work between models and machines.
search_query: arXiv id_list 2505.17716 (LLM agents record and replay)
notes: Primarily a paradigm/design paper; the abstract does not report quantitative results. No peer-reviewed version found.

title: A Novel Zero-Trust Identity Framework for Agentic AI: Decentralized Authentication and Fine-Grained Access Control
venue: 2026 International Conference on AI x Data and Knowledge Engineering (AIxDKE), IEEE
summary: Argues that IAM built for humans or static machine identities (OAuth, OIDC, SAML) is too coarse-grained and single-entity for ephemeral, interdependent agents in multi-agent systems. It proposes an agentic IAM framework built on verifiable agent identities using DIDs and VCs that encode capabilities, provenance, behavioural scope and security posture, plus an Agent Naming Service for discovery, dynamic fine-grained access control, and a unified session-management and policy-enforcement layer for consistent revocation across agent protocols, and discusses zero-knowledge proofs for privacy-preserving attribute disclosure.
relevance: Offers a zero-trust identity and cross-protocol revocation design for agents that move between communication protocols and domains.
search_query: arXiv id_list 2505.19301 (zero-trust identity framework agentic AI)
notes: Published version (Crossref/OpenAlex): IEEE AIxDKE 2026, pp. 98-101, 10 authors including Mahesh Lambe. arXiv 2505.19301 (first posted 2025-05-25; v2 lists 9 authors) is the 24-page preprint; the summary is based on the preprint abstract because no abstract of the 4-page proceedings version was reachable.

title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) at First Glance: Studying the Security and Maintainability of MCP Servers
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (TOSEM)
summary: Presents a large-scale empirical study of 1,899 open-source MCP servers, combining project health metrics with general-purpose static analysis and an MCP-specific scanner. Servers score well on health metrics but the study identifies eight distinct vulnerability types, only three of which overlap with traditional software vulnerabilities, including MCP-specific tool poisoning; 7.2% of servers have general vulnerabilities and 5.5% show tool poisoning, and code smells are common.
relevance: Provides empirical evidence on the quality and safety of the MCP server ecosystem that agents depend on when their tool access moves with them.
search_query: empirical study MCP servers security maintainability
notes: Published in ACM TOSEM (article 3814959, online 2026-05-12; volume/issue not yet assigned in Crossref). arXiv 2506.13538 first posted 2025-06-16; citekey retains 2025.

title: Adaptive AI Agent Placement and Migration in Edge Intelligence Systems
venue: 2025 IEEE 25th International Conference on Communication Technology (ICCT), pp. 1475-1480
summary: The paper deals with deploying LLM-based agents on resource-limited, heterogeneous edge servers. Keeping service quality for mobile users requires migrating these agents, which is complicated because each agent coordinates LLMs, task planning, memory and external tools. The authors propose an adaptive placement and migration framework that models resource, latency and cost constraints and decides with ant colony algorithms plus LLM-based optimisation. Migration is kept lightweight by moving only essential state. A prototype built on AgentScope and tested on globally distributed edge servers is reported to cut deployment latency and migration cost substantially.
relevance: It is a direct modern case of mobile agents for LLMs, in which an agent's essential state is moved between edge hosts.
search_query: abs:"agent migration" AND abs:LLM
notes: Peer-reviewed version in IEEE ICCT 2025 (Shenyang, 16-18 Oct 2025), found by Crossref title search; it has the same title, authors and abstract as arXiv 2508.03345 (posted 2025-08-05).

title: A Survey on the Memory Mechanism of Large Language Model-based Agents
venue: ACM Transactions on Information Systems, vol. 43, no. 6
summary: This survey consolidates scattered work on memory in LLM-based agents. It discusses what agent memory is and why agents need it, reviews how memory modules are designed and evaluated, catalogues applications in which memory is central, and identifies limitations and future directions.
relevance: Provides a taxonomy of agent memory sources, forms and operations that can be used to define which state a portable task context must carry across agents.

notes: Author order differs between the TOIS version (Quanyu Dai second) and arXiv v1 (Dai sixth); the TOIS order from Crossref is used.

title: AIOS: LLM Agent Operating System
venue: Conference on Language Modeling (COLM 2025)
summary: Agents that access LLMs and tools without resource management can waste or misuse resources and cannot run concurrently efficiently. AIOS moves LLM and tool services into a kernel that offers scheduling, context management, memory and storage management and access control to agents, with an SDK for agents built in different frameworks. The authors report up to 2.1x faster execution when serving agents from several frameworks.
relevance: A kernel-level context manager that can save and restore agent context and serve agents from multiple frameworks is a concrete substrate for suspending, relocating and migrating agent runs.
search_query: arXiv id_list 2403.16971; OpenReview search 'AIOS: LLM Agent Operating System'
notes: COLM 2025 acceptance confirmed via arXiv comment and OpenReview (note L4HHkCDz2x). Author order follows the COLM/OpenReview record; arXiv v5 swaps Wenyue Hua and Mingyu Jin. No DOI. date_published approximates the conference month.

title: Open Agent Specification (Agent Spec): A Unified Representation for AI Agents
venue: arXiv preprint
summary: Responds to fragmentation across agent frameworks, which differ in abstractions, data-flow semantics and tool integration, by proposing Agent Spec, a declarative language for defining agents and agentic workflows once and running them on different runtimes. It defines shared components, control- and data-flow semantics and schemas, plus a standardized evaluation harness for comparing behaviour across runtimes. The authors demonstrate it on four runtimes (LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, WayFlow) over three benchmarks and release an SDK, reference runtime and framework adapters.
relevance: The most direct attempt at a framework-neutral agent representation, which is the prerequisite for cross-framework migration of agents and workflows.
search_query: Open Agent Specification Oracle unified representation AI agents
notes: Author list from arXiv v4 (current); an earlier technical-report version indexed by DBLP/OpenReview has a different author list (e.g. includes Vladislav Blinov, Xuelin Situ, Ying Xu). No peer-reviewed version found.

title: Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory
venue: ECAI 2025 (Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence and Applications)
summary: Mem0 is a memory layer for LLM agents that extracts the salient facts from ongoing multi-session conversations, consolidates them and retrieves them later; a variant stores memories as a graph to capture relations between entities. On the LOCOMO benchmark the authors compare it with six baseline categories, including memory-augmented systems, RAG setups, full-context prompting and commercial memory products. Mem0 outperforms the existing memory systems across single-hop, temporal, multi-hop and open-domain questions. Full-context prompting stays slightly more accurate, but Mem0 cuts p95 latency by about 91% and token cost by over 90% compared with it.
relevance: Shows that persistent, externalized memory can be a service decoupled from any single model or session, which is what lets context survive movement between agents and runtimes.

notes: Crossref types the record as a book-chapter in the IOS Press FAIA series; it is the ECAI 2025 proceedings paper.

title: Identity Management for Agentic AI: The new frontier of authorization, authentication, and security for an AI agent world
venue: OpenID Foundation Whitepaper
summary: An OpenID Foundation whitepaper on authentication, authorization and identity management for AI agents. It reviews resources available today for securing agents, using agent-centric protocols such as MCP as a motivating case, and sets out a strategic agenda for longer-term problems including scalable access control, agent-centric identities, distinguishing AI workloads and delegated authority.
relevance: Standards-body view of the identity and delegated-authorization gaps that any cross-agent or cross-organization handoff must close.

notes: Venue taken from the arXiv journal_ref field (OpenID Foundation Whitepaper, 2025).

title: Here Comes the AI Worm: Preventing the Propagation of Adversarial Self-Replicating Prompts Within GenAI Ecosystems
venue: Proceedings of the 2025 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS '25)
summary: The paper shows that when GenAI-powered applications exchange messages and rely on RAG-based inference, an adversarial self-replicating prompt can start a worm-like chain of indirect prompt injections, called RAGworm, in which each compromised application acts maliciously and contaminates the retrieval stores of other applications. In an ecosystem of GenAI email assistants, the authors use it to promote content, spread propaganda and extract confidential data, and they report super-linear spread in which each infected client compromises about 20 others within one to three days. They also study which factors affect the worm's performance. Finally, they propose DonkeyRail, a guardrail that detects and stops propagation with a reported true-positive rate of 1.0, a false-positive rate of 0.017 and only milliseconds of added latency.
relevance: Demonstrates zero-click, multi-hop propagation of malicious context between agents, the worst case for any mechanism that forwards task context or memory between agents.
search_query: Here Comes The AI Worm Morris II zero-click worm GenAI
notes: CCS '25 version, open access (CC BY). Its abstract names the worm 'RAGworm' and the guardrail 'DonkeyRail'. The earlier arXiv preprint 2403.02817 ('Here Comes The AI Worm: Unleashing Zero-click Worms that Target GenAI-Powered Applications') calls them 'Morris-II' and 'Virtual Donkey'. Semantic Scholar/DBLP (conf/ccs/CohenBN25) link the two; the summary follows the CCS abstract.

title: A-Mem: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (NeurIPS 2025)
summary: Existing agent memory systems offer basic storage and retrieval with fixed structures and operations. A-Mem lets the agent organize memory itself following Zettelkasten principles: each new memory becomes a structured note with context, keywords and tags, is linked to related past notes, and can trigger updates to existing notes so the memory network evolves. Experiments across six foundation models report improvements over prior state-of-the-art baselines.
relevance: Self-organizing, linked memory is a candidate format for agent state that must remain coherent when transferred or merged between agents.
search_query: arXiv id_list 2502.12110; OpenReview search 'A-MEM: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents'
notes: NeurIPS 2025 acceptance confirmed via arXiv comment and OpenReview (NeurIPS 2025 poster, note FiM0M8gcct). Proceedings DOI 10.52202/085713-0593 (NeurIPS 38, pp. 20004-20031) per Crossref. Proceedings title uses 'A-Mem'; arXiv uses 'A-MEM'. date_published approximates the conference month.

title: Building A Secure Agentic AI Application Leveraging Google's A2A Protocol
venue: 2025 Annual Computer Security Applications Conference Workshops (ACSAC Workshops)
summary: The paper provides a security analysis of Google's Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, describing its components and operation in the context of agent communication. Using the MAESTRO AI threat-modelling framework, it identifies risks in A2A deployments, with emphasis on Agent Card management, task-execution integrity and authentication. It then recommends secure development practices and architectural patterns, and discusses how combining A2A with MCP can support secure interoperability.
relevance: One of the few peer-reviewed threat models of A2A and agent cards, the delegation protocol at the centre of the agent-movement study.
search_query: Building A Secure Agentic AI Application Leveraging A2A Protocol
notes: Author order and title differ across versions: arXiv lists Habler, Huang, Narajala, Kulkarni and omits "Google's"; the ACSAC Workshops version (Crossref) is used here. Crossref title uses a typographic apostrophe.

title: AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials
venue: Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Agents and Artificial Intelligence (ICAART 2026), Vol. 1
summary: Targets the inability of LLM agents to establish differentiated trust with each other at the start of an agent-to-agent dialogue, especially across organizational boundaries. Presents a conceptual framework and prototype multi-agent system in which each agent holds a ledger-anchored W3C DID and third-party-issued W3C VCs, used to authenticate and to establish cross-domain trust by exchanging credentials. The evaluation shows technical feasibility but also limitations when the agent's LLM alone controls the security procedures.
relevance: Shows a concrete mechanism for verifiable agent identity and trust bootstrapping when work crosses organizational boundaries.

title: SAGA: A Security Architecture for Governing AI Agentic Systems
venue: Proceedings 2026 Network and Distributed System Security Symposium (NDSS 2026)
summary: Notes that prior proposals for agent identity, authorization and delegation are largely theoretical and lack user-controlled agent management. SAGA has users register agents with a central Provider that holds contact information and user-defined access-control policies and helps enforce them on inter-agent communication, using a cryptographic mechanism to derive fine-grained access-control tokens with formal security guarantees. Evaluation across agentic tasks, geolocations and on-device and cloud LLMs reports minimal overhead and no loss of task utility.
relevance: An implemented, evaluated architecture for policy-governed agent-to-agent delegation and lifecycle control.
search_query: arXiv search ti:SAGA AND ti:governing; Crossref query.bibliographic SAGA

title: Intelligent AI Delegation
venue: arXiv preprint
summary: Argues that current task decomposition and delegation among AI agents rely on simple heuristics that cannot adapt to changing environments or robustly handle failures. The authors propose an adaptive framework that treats delegation as a sequence of decisions covering task allocation together with transfer of authority, responsibility and accountability, explicit role and boundary specifications, clarity of intent, and trust-establishment mechanisms. The framework is meant to apply to human and AI delegators and delegatees in delegation networks and to inform protocols for the emerging agentic web.
relevance: Frames delegation as the transfer of authority and accountability, not just a task, which is precisely what an accountable agent handoff must carry.
search_query: Intelligent AI Delegation Tomasev
notes: No peer-reviewed version found via OpenReview search as of 2026-10-15.

title: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design
venue: 2026 IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning (SaTML)
summary: CaMeL wraps an LLM agent in a protective system layer so that it stays secure even if the underlying model is susceptible to prompt injection. It derives the control and data flow from the trusted user query up front, so untrusted data retrieved later cannot change program flow, and attaches capabilities to values so security policies are enforced at tool-call time to block exfiltration over unauthorised flows. On AgentDojo it solves 77% of tasks with provable security versus 84% for an undefended system.
relevance: Capability-tagged data flows are a concrete design for carrying provenance and authorisation along with task context as it moves between agents and tools.
search_query: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design CaMeL
notes: Preprint first posted March 2025; the SaTML 2026 proceedings version confirmed via Crossref.

title: MCPTox: A Benchmark for Tool Poisoning on Real-World MCP Servers
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, vol. 40, no. 42 (AAAI-26)
summary: MCPTox studies tool poisoning, where malicious instructions are hidden in an MCP tool's metadata rather than its outputs, and provides the first systematic benchmark for it, built on live real-world MCP servers and their tools with generated malicious test cases across ten risk categories. Evaluating 20 LLM agent settings, the authors find widespread vulnerability, with more capable models often more susceptible because the attack exploits instruction following, and agents almost never refuse.
relevance: Tool descriptions are part of what an agent ingests when it attaches to new tool servers after moving, so poisoned metadata is a direct risk for relocation and migration.
search_query: MCPTox tool poisoning MCP servers benchmark
notes: arXiv title is 'MCPTox: A Benchmark for Tool Poisoning Attack on Real-World MCP Servers'; AAAI title omits 'Attack'.

title: ACRFence: Preventing Semantic Rollback Attacks in Agent Checkpoint-Restore
venue: arXiv (journal_ref: CoDAIM workshop 2026)
summary: The paper shows that checkpoint-restore in LLM agent frameworks is unsafe because, after a restore, an agent re-generates tool requests that differ slightly from the originals, so servers treat them as new. The authors define this as semantic rollback attacks, identify two classes (Action Replay and Authority Resurrection), and validate them in a proof of concept. They propose ACRFence, a framework-agnostic mitigation that records irreversible tool effects and enforces replay-or-fork semantics on restore.
relevance: It identifies a safety failure unique to resuming LLM agents from checkpoints, which is central to runtime relocation without loss of accountability.
search_query: abs:checkpoint AND abs:"LLM agent" AND abs:migration
notes: The arXiv journal_ref names the CoDAIM workshop 2026, but the workshop proceedings were not confirmed, so it is marked as a preprint and not peer-reviewed.

title: Agentic Context Engineering: Evolving Contexts for Self-Improving Language Models
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2026)
summary: Adapting LLM applications by rewriting their contexts suffers from brevity bias and from context collapse, where repeated rewriting erodes detail. ACE treats contexts as evolving playbooks maintained through generation, reflection and curation, applying structured incremental updates instead of full rewrites. It improves over strong baselines on agent and finance benchmarks in both offline (system prompt) and online (agent memory) settings while lowering adaptation latency and cost, and can learn from execution feedback without labels.
relevance: Treats the agent's context as a structured, incrementally updated artifact, which is the form a portable task context needs in order to be carried and extended by successive agents.
search_query: arXiv id_list 2510.04618; OpenReview search 'Agentic Context Engineering'
notes: ICLR 2026 acceptance confirmed via arXiv comment and OpenReview (venue 'ICLR 2026 Poster'). No DOI. date_published approximates the conference month.

title: Prompt Infection: LLM-to-LLM Prompt Injection within Multi-agent Systems
venue: Computer Security. ESORICS 2025 International Workshops, Lecture Notes in Computer Science (Springer)
summary: The paper shows that prompt injection can spread between LLM agents in a multi-agent system: an injected prompt copies itself from agent to agent, so the attack moves through the system like a computer virus. This adds data propagation and self-replication to ordinary prompt injection, and it can enable data theft, scams, misinformation and system-wide disruption. The published version reports that existing prompt-injection defenses, adapted for multi-agent use, reduce how far the infection spreads. The earlier arXiv preprint frames its defense as LLM Tagging, which marks agent-originated messages, used together with existing safeguards.

title: MCP safety audit: LLMs with the model context protocol allow major security exploits
venue: Assurance and Security for AI-enabled Systems 2026 (Proceedings of SPIE)
summary: The paper argues that the MCP design exposes end users to serious risks and demonstrates that leading LLMs can be induced, through MCP tools, to compromise a developer's machine via malicious code execution, remote access control and credential theft. As a mitigation it introduces MCPSafetyScanner, an agentic auditing tool that generates adversarial samples from an MCP server's tools and resources, searches for related vulnerabilities and remediations, and produces a security report before deployment.
relevance: Shows that the tool-access layer agents rely on after a handoff or relocation is itself an attack vector and offers a pre-deployment audit approach for MCP servers.

title: ACON: Optimizing Context Compression for Long-horizon LLM Agents
venue: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Long-horizon agents accumulate unbounded histories that raise inference memory cost and degrade reasoning. ACON compresses both observations and interaction history by iteratively refining natural-language compression guidelines from analysis of agent failures, without fine-tuning the agent, and then distils the compressor into smaller models. On AppWorld, OfficeBench and multi-objective QA it reduces peak token usage by 26-54% while improving task success over compression baselines.
relevance: Compressing agent history while preserving critical state is exactly the problem of producing a compact, transferable task context for handoff or resumption.

title: Model Context Protocol (MCP): Landscape, Security Threats, and Future Research Directions
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology, vol. 35, no. 10
summary: This study examines MCP from architectural and security perspectives, defining an MCP server lifecycle of four phases (creation, deployment, operation, maintenance) broken into 16 activities. On that basis it builds a threat taxonomy across four attacker types (malicious developers, external attackers, malicious users and security flaws) covering 16 threat scenarios, validated with real-world case studies. It then proposes phase- and threat-specific safeguards and surveys MCP adoption and tooling to identify limitations and research directions.

title: Design issues in mobile agent programming systems
venue: IEEE Concurrency
summary: The article discusses the system-level issues and agent-programming requirements that arise in the design of mobile agent systems, and describes several existing systems to illustrate the different approaches their designers took. The issues covered include agent mobility and naming; security, privacy and integrity; authentication, authorization and access control; metering and charging; and programming primitives for agent communication and synchronization, for monitoring and control, and for fault tolerance.
relevance: It lists in one place the design questions a relocatable agent runtime has to settle (naming, authority at the destination, monitoring and control of an agent that has moved, fault tolerance), which recur for any mechanism that relocates LLM-agent work.

title: Closing the AI accountability gap: defining an end-to-end framework for internal algorithmic auditing
venue: Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAT* '20)
summary: The authors observe that rising concern about AI has produced a wave of academic and journalistic work auditing deployed systems for harm from outside the deploying organizations, while practitioners still find it hard to identify the harmful consequences of their own systems before deployment, and emergent issues can be difficult or impossible to trace back to their source afterwards. They introduce a framework for internal algorithmic auditing that supports AI system development end to end and is applied throughout the organization's development lifecycle. Each audit stage yields documents that together form an overall audit report, drawing on the organization's values or principles to assess the decisions made, with the aim of helping to close the accountability gap in developing and deploying large-scale AI systems.
relevance: Its stage-by-stage audit record is a model for the accountability trail that would have to travel with agent work, so that a problem surfacing after a handoff can still be traced to its source.

title: Harms from Increasingly Agentic Algorithmic Systems
venue: 2023 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT '23)
summary: Argues that the fairness, accountability, transparency and ethics community should anticipate harms from increasingly agentic algorithmic systems rather than only respond to them. Instead of defining agency as a binary property, it identifies four characteristics that, particularly in combination, increase a system's agency: underspecification, directness of impact, goal-directedness and long-term planning. It discusses harms that arise from increasing agency, notably systemic and long-range impacts that often fall on marginalized or unconsidered stakeholders, and stresses that recognizing such agency does not absolve or shift human responsibility for those harms.
relevance: The four characteristics give a vocabulary for how much autonomy is handed over when a task is delegated or moved to another agent, and the paper's position that responsibility stays with humans bears on who remains accountable after a handoff.

title: TaskWeaver: A Code-First Agent Framework
venue: arXiv preprint
summary: Presents TaskWeaver, a code-first framework for building LLM-powered autonomous agents, motivated by the limits of existing LLM frameworks on domain-specific data-analytics tasks with rich data structures and on meeting diverse user requirements flexibly. TaskWeaver converts user requests into executable code and treats user-defined plugins as callable functions, with support for rich data structures, flexible plugin use and dynamic plugin selection. It incorporates domain-specific knowledge through examples and, according to the authors, ensures secure execution of the generated code; the framework is open source.
relevance: Expressing an agent's work as generated code plus plugin calls makes explicit the tool surface that would have to be re-granted when that work is delegated or moved to another runtime.

title: Identifying the Risks of LM Agents with an LM-Emulated Sandbox
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2024), spotlight
summary: Introduces ToolEmu, a framework that uses a language model to emulate tool execution, so that LM agents can be tested against a diverse range of tools and scenarios without implementing the tools or setting up each test environment by hand. An LM-based automatic safety evaluator examines agent failures and quantifies the associated risks; in human evaluation, 68.8% of failures identified with ToolEmu were judged to be valid real-world agent failures. On an initial benchmark of 36 high-stakes toolkits (311 tools in total) and 144 test cases, even the safest LM agent exhibited such failures 23.9% of the time according to the evaluator.
relevance: An emulated sandbox lets an agent's tool behaviour be probed before it is granted real tools, a candidate admission check for an agent that has been delegated work or moved to a new environment.

title: Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents
venue: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
summary: Proposes Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA), a conceptual framework drawing on cognitive science and symbolic AI to organize LLM-based language agents. CoALA describes an agent in terms of modular memory components, a structured action space for interacting with internal memory and external environments, and a generalized decision-making process for choosing actions. The authors use it to survey and organize a large body of recent work retrospectively and to identify actionable directions towards more capable agents.

title: Agent Smith: A Single Image Can Jailbreak One Million Multimodal LLM Agents Exponentially Fast
venue: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2024), PMLR 235
summary: Reports a safety issue in multi-agent environments called infectious jailbreak: an adversary jailbreaks a single multimodal LLM agent and, without further intervention, (almost) all agents become infected exponentially fast and exhibit harmful behaviours. In simulated environments of up to one million LLaVA-1.5 agents interacting through randomized pair-wise chat, feeding an adversarial image into the memory of any randomly chosen agent was sufficient to achieve infectious jailbreak. The authors derive a simple principle for determining whether a defense can provably restrain the spread, and leave the design of a practical defense that meets it as an open question.
relevance: Shows that content held in agent memory and exchanged between agents can spread a compromise across a population, so any context that moves with a task has to be treated as untrusted at every hop.
